attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, given as a rebuttal to the graph's 'smart high schooler' label.

semantics.note: Keeps the better/worse comparison with a smart high schooler and the absolute claim 'very few reliably'. Unhedged present-tense observation.

contract.note: The plain reading (uneven abilities, dependable on only a small minority of tasks) is ordinary and fair. Marcus set no threshold or task population for 'very few', so the result depends on the evaluator's sampling frame.

evidence.note: OpenAI disclosure from March 2023 admitting GPT-4 is not fully reliable. Consistent with the claim, but it gives no share of tasks performed reliably and describes the original release.

OpenAI technical report showing strong exam scores and weak scores on some exams. Shows strengths and weaknesses, but exam percentiles do not measure repeated reliability or compare against a defined group of smart students.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only company disclosures from 2023. They show uneven abilities and admitted unreliability, but nothing measures how many tasks GPT-4 did reliably in June 2024 against capable students. The strong exam results do not show broad reliability either, so the evidence settles neither the support nor the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own critique of Aschenbrenner's graph, in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful wording. 'Makes no sense' is evaluative. 'Presupposes its own conclusion' is a checkable claim about how the graph was built, so treating it as an observation is acceptable.

contract.note: The contract sets aside 'makes no sense' as evaluative and tests whether the human-capability axis is assigned by assumption rather than independently calibrated. That is a fair, ordinary reading of 'presupposes', but the result depends on it.

evidence.note: Aschenbrenner's own essay, where he urges readers to trust the trendline. This is the primary text, though it is labelled a secondary summary. It shows he relies on trend extrapolation, but the excerpt does not show how the capability axis was mapped or calibrated.

reviews.rationale: The only item shows trend extrapolation but not how compute was mapped to human stages, nor whether that mapping was calibrated independently. The packet also notes it does not settle whether the analogy was meant as an illustration or as proof. It meets neither condition. 'Makes no sense' is evaluative and is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'I can't think of' qualifier and limits scope to models existing by the post. The 'Marcus says' wording could be read as true by definition, but the contract tests the underlying factual claim. That qualifier limits what he claims to know; it is not a probability hedge.

contract.note: Testing whether any comparable measure exists, using only models available by June 5, 2024, is a fair reading. Undefined terms (which measure, what counts as outpacing, the 2020 baseline, 'behind the curve') mean the evaluator's interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: Google disclosure from February 2024 of a 1M-token context window. A possible counterexample under a broad reading, but the packet gives no GPT-4 or 2020 figures for a three-point comparison.
2020 MMLU baselines. Useful for choosing the 2020 leader, but supplies no 2024 model comparison against GPT-4.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no like-for-like comparison of a 2020 leader, GPT-4 and a 2024 model. The context-window figure would need GPT-4's baseline, which is missing, and it may not count as a relevant measure. Nothing shows that no qualifying measure exists, and no trajectory is given for 'behind the curve'. Neither condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own critique of Aschenbrenner's graph.

semantics.note: Faithful. It lists the trend assumption and each obstacle he says was ignored. Marcus wrote 'the fact that' synthetic data may be less useful; the drafter's 'possibility' softens this slightly but does not matter here.

contract.note: Reading the graph together with its accompanying analysis, and 'ignoring' as not discussing, is an ordinary reading. Marcus could have meant the plotted line does not account for the obstacles; the contract notes that discussing an obstacle is not the same as building it in numerically.

evidence.note: Aschenbrenner's own text tells readers to trust the trendline. Supports the claim that the graph assumes continued progress.
The data-wall section discusses running out of data, a possible plateau, and synthetic data as a workaround. Rebuts the claim that data limits were ignored.
The linked infrastructure essay names power as the biggest supply constraint. Rebuts the claim that energy limits were ignored.

reviews.rationale: The part about assuming continued progress holds: the analysis extrapolates the trend. The claim that data and energy limits were ignored fails, because the accompanying analysis discusses the data wall and power constraints explicitly. The packet does not settle the treatment of hallucinations, planning and reasoning. Whether the obstacles were built into the forecast numerically is also not shown.
